title: FTC and 20 States Sue Dollar General Over Alleged Customer Overcharging Scandal
body:
The Federal Trade Commission and a coalition of 20 state attorneys general sued Dollar General on Monday, accusing the discount retailer of systematically inflating prices and charging vulnerable shoppers for items that were never stocked on shelves. The complaint alleges that the chain’s “price‑tagging” scheme—where advertised prices were applied to out‑of‑stock or “back‑room” inventory—cost consumers millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges, violating federal and state consumer‑protection laws.

According to the filing, Dollar General used a “price‑tagging” practice that misled shoppers into believing that advertised low‑price items were available for purchase on the sales floor. In reality, many of these items were hidden in the store’s backroom, and cashiers were instructed to “price‑match” the advertised price even when the product was not physically present. The FTC’s investigation, which began in 2021, uncovered internal documents and employee testimonies indicating that the practice was intentional and widespread, affecting thousands of stores across the United States. The lawsuit seeks civil penalties, restitution for affected customers, and an injunction to halt the deceptive pricing scheme.

Consumer‑advocacy groups have long warned that low‑income shoppers are disproportionately harmed by such tactics, as they rely on discount retailers for essential goods. “When a retailer advertises a bargain and then denies the sale at the checkout, it’s not just a pricing error—it’s an exploitation of trust, especially for those with limited alternatives,” said Maria Torres, director of the Consumer Justice Alliance. The complaint highlights that Dollar General’s alleged conduct may have targeted neighborhoods with higher concentrations of low‑income families, raising concerns about discriminatory impacts that could violate the Federal Trade Commission Act and state consumer‑protection statutes.

Dollar General, which operates more than 19,000 stores in 48 states, has denied the allegations and vowed to defend itself vigorously. In a statement released after the filing, the company called the lawsuit “unfounded” and asserted that its pricing policies comply with all applicable laws. The retailer also noted that it has instituted “enhanced compliance training” for employees and is reviewing its inventory management systems. However, the FTC’s complaint suggests that the alleged overcharges could total as much as $1.2 billion, a figure that, if proven, would represent one of the largest consumer‑protection settlements in the retail sector.

Legal experts see this case as a bellwether for the broader fight against deceptive pricing in the discount‑store industry, which has grown rapidly amid inflationary pressures. “The FTC is sending a clear signal that aggressive cost‑cutting cannot come at the expense of transparent pricing,” said Jonathan Meyers, a professor of antitrust law at Georgetown University. The involvement of 20 states amplifies the pressure on Dollar General, as coordinated multi‑jurisdictional actions can lead to substantial penalties and mandatory reforms. Moreover, the case may prompt other retailers to audit their own pricing practices to avoid similar litigation.

The outcome of the lawsuit could reshape how discount retailers display and honor advertised prices, potentially spurring industry‑wide changes in inventory visibility and point‑of‑sale verification. As the case moves forward, consumers and regulators will be watching closely for any settlement terms that mandate restitution and stricter oversight. For now, the legal battle underscores the growing scrutiny of big‑box retailers and the importance of protecting shoppers—especially those most vulnerable—from hidden costs hidden behind seemingly low‑price tags.
